title: THEY LOWERED JEREMIAH INTO THE MUD TO SILENCE HIM—BUT GOD HAD NOT FINISHED WRITING HIS STORY
paragraphs: THEY LOWERED JEREMIAH INTO THE MUD TO SILENCE HIM—BUT GOD HAD NOT FINISHED WRITING HIS STORY

He told the truth God gave him. They hated him for it. Then the ropes lowered him into darkness, his feet disappeared into the mud, and the prophet discovered something every wounded believer eventually has to learn: being abandoned by people does not mean you have been abandoned by God.
There is a particular kind of pain that comes when you suffer not because you betrayed God...
but because you obeyed Him.
Jeremiah knew that pain.
Imagine the moment.
Jerusalem is dying.

Babylon is closing in. Hunger is tightening its hands around the city. Political leaders are desperate. Fear is everywhere. And in the middle of that collapsing world stands one inconvenient prophet with an inconvenient message.
Jeremiah.
He does not tell the rulers what they want to hear.
He tells them what God has said.
And sometimes truth becomes most offensive when people have built their lives around avoiding it.
The officials hear Jeremiah's words and decide that the problem is not their rebellion.
The problem, apparently, is Jeremiah.
That is one of sin's oldest tricks.
When truth exposes us, we can repent...
or we can attack the messenger.
They chose the messenger.
King Zedekiah, weak and frightened, effectively surrendered Jeremiah into their hands.
Then came the ropes.
Jeremiah 38:6 preserves the scene with almost unbearable simplicity:
"וּבַבּוֹר אֵין־מַיִם כִּי אִם־טִיט וַיִּטְבַּע יִרְמְיָהוּ בַּטִּיט"
Uvabbor ein-mayim ki im-tit, wayyiṭbaʿ Yirmeyahu baṭṭit.
A close rendering is:
"In the cistern there was no water, but only mud, and Jeremiah sank in the mud."
Do not rush past that last word.
טִיט — ṭit.
Mud. Mire.
And the verb וַיִּטְבַּע — wayyiṭbaʿ — means that Jeremiah sank.
They did not merely put him into a comfortable underground prison.
They lowered him by ropes into a cistern where there was no water, only mire.
Then they left him there.
Try to feel the story before turning it into a sermon.
Feel the rope against his body.
Feel his feet touch the bottom.
Then sink.
Ankles.
Calves.
Perhaps deeper.
Cold mud gripping his legs.
Walls rising around him.
Daylight somewhere above.
No staircase.
No escape.
No crowd applauding the prophet for being faithful.
No visible miracle yet.
Just mud.
And perhaps that is where this story stops feeling ancient.
Because some of you know exactly what it means to obey God and still end up in something that feels like a pit.
You prayed...
and the marriage still broke.
You forgave...
and they still walked away.
You tried to live clean...
and temptation still followed you home.
You told the truth...
and somehow you became the villain.
You served people who disappeared when you needed them.
You poured yourself into a family that barely notices how tired you are.
You kept smiling at church while privately wondering how much longer your soul could carry what nobody else could see.
You thought obedience would keep you out of the mud.
Jeremiah teaches us otherwise.
Faithfulness does not guarantee a painless life.
Sometimes faithfulness is exactly what puts you in conflict with a world that does not want God's truth.
But listen carefully:
The cistern was not proof that God had abandoned Jeremiah.
And your pit is not automatically proof that God has abandoned you.
There are seasons when God's presence is not demonstrated by immediate escape.
Sometimes His faithfulness is revealed by the fact that the pit does not get the final sentence.
Jeremiah could not climb out.
That matters.
We live in a culture obsessed with telling wounded people to rescue themselves.
Believe in yourself.
Find your strength.
Manifest your future.
Become your own salvation.
But Jeremiah had mud beneath him and walls around him.
He needed someone from above to intervene.
And that is where an unexpected man enters the story.
Not one of Jerusalem's powerful officials.
Not one of the men who had protected Jeremiah's reputation.
A Cushite named Ebed-melech.
When Ebed-melech hears what has happened, he goes to the king and calls the act what it is: evil.
Then the king authorizes a rescue.
And suddenly ropes descend into the darkness again.
Think about that.
The first ropes lowered Jeremiah toward death.
The next ropes were coming to lift him toward life.
Same prophet.
Same pit.
Different purpose.
And Scripture records a strangely tender detail.
Ebed-melech does not simply throw down ropes and shout, "Grab on."
He brings old rags and worn-out cloths and tells Jeremiah to place them under his armpits beneath the ropes.
Why?
Because rescue did not have to become another wound.
There is something beautiful here.
God's providence can arrive through ordinary things.
Old cloth.
Ropes.
A courageous servant.
Hands willing to pull.
No thunder.
No fire falling from heaven.
No angel visibly splitting the sky.
Just mercy entering the pit through someone willing to act.

Some of us keep waiting for God to rescue us spectacularly while overlooking the people, Scripture, conviction, church community, unexpected phone call, quiet provision, or ordinary act of compassion He has already placed above the cistern.
And sometimes...
you are Ebed-melech.
Someone you know is sinking.
They still post pictures.
Still answer, "I'm okay."
Still attend church.
Still go to work.
Still laugh.
But underneath everything, they are exhausted.
Their faith is hanging by threads.
Their marriage is hurting.
Their secret sin is consuming them.
Their grief is suffocating them.
Their prayers have become shorter because they no longer know what to say.
Maybe they do not need another person standing above the pit explaining why they should have avoided it.
Maybe they need someone willing to lower a rope.
This is why sharing the Gospel matters.
This is why telling someone about Jesus matters.
This is why checking on the person God suddenly puts on your heart matters.
Someone is sitting in darkness wondering whether anybody knows they are there.
Your obedience may become the rope God uses.
But Jeremiah's cistern points beyond Jeremiah.
Because centuries later, another righteous sufferer would be rejected for speaking truth.
Jesus Christ.
Jeremiah was hated by leaders who did not want his message.
Jesus "came unto his own, and his own received him not" (John 1:11).
Jeremiah was handed over by a compromised ruler.
Jesus stood before Pontius Pilate while political pressure and human fear surrounded His condemnation.
Jeremiah descended into a place from which he could not rescue himself.
Jesus willingly descended all the way into death.
But here the comparison must remain careful.
Jeremiah was a prophet who needed rescue.
Jesus is the Savior who came to rescue sinners.
Jeremiah suffered because he faithfully proclaimed God's word.
Christ did something infinitely greater: He bore our sins in His body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24).
The Gospel is not that Jesus came merely to inspire wounded people.
He came to save sinners.
Our deepest cistern is not depression, betrayal, poverty, rejection, addiction, loneliness, or failure—terrible as those things can be.
Our deepest problem is sin.
Sin separates.
Sin deceives.
Sin hardens.
Sin makes us hide from God while convincing us that hiding is freedom.
And eventually sin pays its terrible wage: death.
That is why Christianity cannot be reduced to "God will get you through difficult times."
The Gospel is far more glorious.
Christ came because we needed forgiveness.
We needed reconciliation.
We needed redemption.
We needed Someone to do for us what we could never accomplish for ourselves.
At the cross, Jesus did not merely sympathize with sinners trapped in the pit.
He gave Himself for them.
He was crucified.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose.
The stone did not keep Him.
Death did not keep Him.
The grave did not write the ending.
Jesus did.
That is why grace can reach you wherever you are reading this.
Even if your life feels muddy.
Even if you made the decisions that brought you there.
Even if your pit was not caused by faithfulness like Jeremiah's but by your own rebellion.
That distinction matters.
Sometimes we suffer because we obeyed God.
Sometimes we suffer because we ignored Him.
Sometimes we suffer simply because we live in a fallen world.
But none of those realities places a repentant sinner beyond the reach of Christ.
Maybe your mud has a name.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Pride.
Alcohol.
Secret messages.
An affair nobody knows about.
Jealousy.
Greed.
Religious hypocrisy.
Unforgiveness.
A double life.
Maybe you have become frighteningly good at appearing spiritually alive while something inside you is slowly sinking.
You know the Christian vocabulary.
You know when to say "Amen."
You know which verse to post.
You know how to lift your hands.
But when the room becomes quiet and there is nobody left to impress...
you know.
You know where the mud is.
And Jesus knows too.
Yet the shocking message of the Gospel is not that Christ waits above the pit laughing at filthy people.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He offers mercy.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He restores.
He makes new.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is turning from the mud because you finally believe Jesus is better.
Grace does not tell you the mud is clean.
Grace tells you that you do not have to die there.
That is the scandal.
Holy God receiving guilty people.
The spotless Christ dying for sinners.
The condemned being forgiven.
The ashamed being clothed in righteousness they could never earn.
The rebel becoming a child of God through faith in Jesus Christ.
The person everyone else wrote off becoming living evidence that God is still writing.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending your past never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by erasing the seriousness of sin.
He rewrites everything by redeeming what sin meant to destroy.
Look at Jeremiah again.
The men who lowered him apparently expected the cistern to silence him.
Yet thousands of years later, we are still reading his words.
The mud could not erase the message.
The pit could not cancel the calling.
The people who wanted Jeremiah forgotten are remembered largely because Scripture records what they did to Jeremiah.
And the prophet they tried to silence still speaks.
That should make somebody reading this reconsider the chapter you thought destroyed your story.
Your betrayal may not be the final chapter.
Your relapse does not have to be the final chapter.
Your divorce does not have to be the final chapter.
Your shame does not have to be the final chapter.
Your grief does not have to be the final chapter.
Your failure does not have to be the final chapter.
Your past does not possess authorship rights over your future.
Jesus does not promise that every earthly consequence disappears when we come to Him.
He promises something greater than cosmetic repair.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation with God.
New life.
His presence.
A new identity rooted not in what we have done but in what Christ has done for those who trust Him.
And perhaps the most dangerous thing about a pit is that after enough time in darkness, you begin believing darkness is where you belong.
No.
Hear the Gospel.
You may have fallen.
You may have failed.
You may have sinned horribly.
You may have wounds nobody understands.
But if you can still hear Christ calling you to repent and come to Him, the story is not over.
Stop decorating the cistern.
Stop defending the mud.
Stop calling bondage personality.
Stop calling compromise freedom.
Stop waiting until you feel worthy enough to approach Jesus.
You will never climb high enough to deserve Calvary.
Come because He is merciful.
Come because His blood is sufficient.
Come because sinners are exactly the people He came to save.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come empty-handed.
Be honest.
And if God has already brought you out of a pit you thought would bury you, tell somebody what Jesus has done.
Your testimony might become another person's rope.
Send it privately to the person who has gone unusually silent.

Supporting Gospel work financially or through sharing is one way believers may freely participate in ministry, but it should never be confused with earning God's approval or proving that you glorify Him. We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ; when you freely support sound Gospel ministry, you help that ministry place biblical resources before more people.
Jesus Christ.
Not the platform.
Not the merchandise.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Jesus.
Because Jeremiah's story is not ultimately an advertisement for positive thinking.
It is a witness that human beings do not possess the final word over what God purposes to do.
And the Gospel takes that truth to its blazing center.
They rejected Christ.
Mocked Him.
Stripped Him.
Nailed Him to a cross.
Watched Him die.
Sealed His tomb.
And human history seemed to place a period where God had written a comma.
Then came Sunday.
The grave opened.
Christ rose.
And ever since, every sinner who comes to Him in repentance and faith can know that shame does not have to write the ending.
Maybe tonight you feel the mud around your feet.
Maybe you cannot see the rope yet.
Maybe you cannot imagine how God could possibly redeem what has happened.
Jeremiah could not see through the walls of his cistern either.
But above him, while he was still in the mud, God was already moving through a man named Ebed-melech.
You do not have to see everything God is doing to trust the God who sees you.
So cry if you need to.
Confess what needs confessing.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Ask for help.
Reach for the rope.
And above everything else...
reach for Christ.
Because sometimes the chapter that looks most like your burial becomes the chapter you later point to and whisper:
"That was where I discovered He had not abandoned me."
The mud may explain where you have been—but because of Jesus, it does not get to decide who you become.
